cleo_hotel.png.note: Real plan. Captions are English plus one misspelled French word (RÉGÉPTION), and a demo heatmap is baked into the image. 'restroom' is the check that needs vision rather than caption transcription: the bathrooms are drawn as unlabelled fixtures. NOT a hold-out — this is also the E2E fixture, so it is the most overfit input in the repo.

cafe_vector.pdf.note: Synthetic but measured: double-line walls, door swing arcs, furniture, scale bar, 1:100 title block. Generated from an explicit room model, so every caption is provably inside its own room.

coworking_vector.pdf.note: Second venue type. The exterior door is drawn on the reception's south wall, so expect_entrance is evidenced by the drawing rather than inferred.

sales_chart.png.note: Bar chart. Intake must reject it AND say why in a sentence — accepting this is the product's worst failure mode, so both of its checks are hard.

blackstone_hotel_1910.png.note: A REAL HOLD-OUT: the Blackstone Hotel, Chicago (Marshall & Fox, c.1910), public domain via Wikimedia Commons. Nothing about this product influenced it — unlike cleo_hotel.png, which is also the E2E fixture. Four floor plates on one sheet, which is normal architectural practice and which used to blow the Zone Analyst's token budget outright; the prompt now scopes to the ground/entrance plate. Period labels (Lounging Room, Buffet, Ball Room, Cigar Stand) test function-not-wording classification on vocabulary no modern plan uses. Its retail concessions (Flower Shop, Shop, Barber Shop) are why ZoneCategory gained a `retail` value on 2026-08-08 — they had been landing in `other`, taking a default attraction in the flow simulation and a default floor share in the solver. This plan now REQUIRES retail, which is the check that would catch the category being dropped or the analyst forgetting it exists. A small allowance remains for the double-height voids ("Upper Part of…"), which genuinely are not floor zones.

park_lane_ground.png.note: Park Lane Hotel, London (Hotel Monthly, Chicago, Vol 35 No 410, May 1927, p.62). Public domain, verified through the Wikimedia Commons API rather than taken on trust: LicenseShortName 'Public domain', Restrictions none. A SECOND HOLD-OUT, and the ground floor of the same property as park_lane_guestfloor.png — the pairing is the point, because a hotel's public floor and its bedroom floor read completely differently and the benchmark had only ever seen public floors. Every required category is printed on the drawing in period capitals: PICADILLY ENTRANCE HALL, LOUNGE, GRILL ROOM, RESTAURANT, TEA ROOM, SMOKING ROOM, and SHOP 1 through SHOP 6 along the Piccadilly frontage. Those six shops are why `retail` is required here: it is the most retail-dense plan in the set, so a dropped category cannot hide. The allowance covers the areas and light wells, which are not floor zones. Counting correction: the range was first written as 8-24 by estimate and the plan read 29, so the label was wrong, not the product — counting the printed rooms gives six shops, entrance hall, lounge, grill room, service, restaurant, tea room, smoking room, south and service entrances, plus stairs, lifts, cloaks and telephone rooms, which lands in the thirties once circulation is included. Known imperfection, recorded rather than tuned away: the analyst leaves two or three Piccadilly-frontage staircases out of the adjacency list. It has no client-visible effect here because stairs are utility zones, excluded from both the score and the dead-zone list. It is deliberately NOT repaired by connecting orphans to their nearest neighbour: inferring adjacency from proximity would join rooms through walls and route simulated guests through solid masonry, which is a worse answer than an unlinked staircase. The orphan set is unstable in the same way: one run left three Piccadilly staircases unlinked, the next left a back aisle, a cafe-luncheon room and a service restroom. That it varies is the point — it is model judgement about doorways on a grainy 1927 scan, not a deterministic defect, and it stays a soft check for that reason.

park_lane_guestfloor.png.note: Same source and licence as park_lane_ground.png, and THE PLAN CLASS THE BENCHMARK NEVER HAD: a typical guest-room floor, roughly twenty bedrooms with ensuites off double-loaded corridors around a light well. This is the exact shape that exposed the missing `guestroom` category on 2026-08-08 — before that fix every room here landed in `other` and drew the flow simulation's default attraction of 1.0 against dining's 5.0, so the simulation routed guests away from the only real destination on the floor. `guestroom` is required for the same reason `retail` is required on the Blackstone: it is the check that fails loudly if the category is ever dropped. Note on `expect_entrance`: a typical floor has no door to the street, and what the analyst marks is the lift and stair arrival point. That is the correct answer for flow purposes — it is where guests enter the floor — but it is why the flow step reports falling back to distance decay here, which the report discloses. Observed variance, recorded rather than hidden: two benchmark runs of the identical file on identical code read 33 zones and then 43. The categorical checks were stable across both — guestroom, corridor and the entrance were found every time — so what moves is how finely the analyst subdivides a repetitive bedroom floor, chiefly whether an ensuite is folded into its room or split out. The range is therefore set to catch GROSS failure (a handful of zones, or a hundred) and not to pin an exact count, because on a forty-room plan an exact count is not a property a vision model can be held to. Tightening it would produce a benchmark that cries wolf, and a check that fails at random is worse than no check, because the next real failure gets re-run instead of read.

commodore_perry_basement.png.note:
Commodore Perry Hotel, Toledo (Hotel Monthly, Vol 35 No 411, June 1927). Public domain, verified through the Wikimedia Commons API: LicenseShortName 'Public domain', Restrictions none. Same trade-press family as the Park Lane pair.

THE BACK-OF-HOUSE PLAN THE BENCHMARK LACKED. Every other plan in this set is a public floor; this is a hotel basement and nothing else — kitchen, kitchen stores, cold rooms for fruit, dairy, delicatessen and meat, laundry, steward's office, staff cafeterias and locker rooms, boiler and machinery plant, garbage sorting, soiled linen. It is the densest labelled service floor found anywhere, and it is why `kitchen`, `storage` and `service` are required here and nowhere else.

KNOWN LIMITATION THIS PLAN MAKES VISIBLE, recorded rather than hidden: the flow-efficiency score decides guest-facing by category, and category is function, not audience. On this floor the staff cafeterias read as `dining`, the engineers' and switchboard rooms as `workspace`, the service hall as `corridor` and the areaway as `entrance` — all correct descriptions, all scored as though guests used them. A studio uploading a service floor would get a plausible number computed over staff space. Fixing it needs a staff-versus-guest distinction in the taxonomy, which is a product decision rather than a bug fix, so the labels here assert only what the drawing states and this note carries the rest. The zone range is wide because a forty-room service floor is exactly where a vision model's subdivision varies most.
